title: Efficient characterization of instance-optimal identity testing
formal:
Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(\Phi\) and a universal constant \(C\ge1\) such that, for every explicitly given finite rational probability vector \(q\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\le1\),
\[C^{-1}n_*(q,\varepsilon)\le\Phi(q,\varepsilon)\le Cn_*(q,\varepsilon)?\]
The integer \(n_*(q,\varepsilon)\) is the smallest fixed number of independent samples needed to distinguish \(p=q\) from \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon\), with each error probability at most \(1/3\), when the reference \(q\) is known and the unknown distribution \(p\) is otherwise arbitrary. Computation of the statistical test is unrestricted. Polynomial time is required of the evaluator of the characterization, in the binary input length of \((q,\varepsilon)\), and the multiplicative constant must hold at the same input \(\varepsilon\).

This is the finite, explicitly encoded version of the efficient-computability branch of the source's Open Question 1. The source also allows countably infinite domains and leaves “succinct” open to a closed-form interpretation; this card makes its computational interpretation and finite rational input scope explicit rather than treating those broader interpretations as equivalent.
why: Two reference distributions on the same domain can require very different numbers of samples to test. A computable characterization at the exact requested distance would identify the information needed for each reference profile, including distributions for which existing bounds disagree by unbounded factors. It would also separate the statistical cost of testing from the cost of evaluating that cost.

sentences: The problem asks for an efficiently computable estimate of the optimal sample count for testing equality to a particular known distribution.
The selected variant gives the reference probabilities and distance threshold explicitly as binary rational numbers.
The estimate must match the information-theoretic optimum within one universal factor at exactly the requested distance.
Existing instance-dependent bounds can disagree by arbitrarily large factors because their distance parameters differ.
The card makes efficient evaluation precise while keeping the computation of the statistical test unrestricted.

definitions:
For an integer \(d\ge1\), write \([d]=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) and \(\Delta_d=\{p\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{d}:\sum_i p_i=1\}\). The input lists every entry of \(q\in\Delta_d\cap\mathbb Q^d\), including zeros, and the rational number \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\). Rationals are represented by binary nonnegative numerators and positive denominators in lowest terms, with delimiters; let \(B\) be the total bit length, including the length encoding of the list. No oracle or compressed description replaces this list. The alternative \(p\) ranges over all of \(\Delta_d\), including irrational probabilities and mass on coordinates where \(q_i=0\). Total variation is
\[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{d}|p_i-q_i|.\]

For a nonnegative integer \(s\), a possibly randomized statistical test is specified by a function \(\tau:[d]^s\to[0,1]\); \(\tau(x)\) is its conditional probability of rejecting the null on sample sequence \(x\). There is no time, space or representation constraint on this finite table of real probabilities. The product law \(p^{\otimes s}\) means that all \(s\) observations are independent and have law \(p\). A valid test satisfies
\[\mathbb E_{q^{\otimes s}}\tau\le1/3,\qquad
\forall p\in\Delta_d\text{ with }d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)>\varepsilon:\quad \mathbb E_{p^{\otimes s}}\tau\ge2/3.\]
The same test must work for every alternative at that fixed \((q,\varepsilon)\); it cannot be chosen after learning \(p\). The minimum such \(s\) defines \(n_*\). It is finite on every permitted input. The sample count is fixed in advance, not an expected stopping time, and the two errors are bounded separately. Cases with \(0<d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,q)\le\varepsilon\) impose no condition.

The zero-sample case is included: \([d]^0\) is a singleton. The alternative is empty exactly when \(\varepsilon\ge1-\min_iq_i\), since the largest possible distance from \(q\) in this simplex is \(1-\min_iq_i\). In that case \(n_*=0\); otherwise \(n_*\ge1\). Thus the claimed multiplicative guarantee requires the evaluator to return exactly zero in empty-alternative cases, including \(d=1\). The strict inequality in the alternative is intentional.

The evaluator is a single finite-program deterministic multitape Turing machine. It outputs a nonnegative integer in binary and halts within \(K(B+1)^a\) steps for some fixed constants \(K,a\), independent of \(d,q,\varepsilon\); input reading, bit arithmetic and output writing all count. It has no advice or oracles, and must halt within the same bound on malformed encodings, whose outputs are irrelevant. The quantifier order is existence of the evaluator and constants, followed by all valid inputs. There is no permission for polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) in place of polynomial dependence on its encoded length. The statistical tester whose existence defines \(n_*\) is a separate object and need not be produced by this evaluator.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed existence claim. A positive answer must specify the evaluator and prove its uniform polynomial running time and both bounds with one universal finite factor \(C\). A negative answer must refute the existence of every such evaluator and constant; failure of one proposed expression is insufficient. Neither defining \(\Phi\) by the minimum over all statistical tests without proving efficient evaluation, nor comparing upper and lower bounds at different multiples of \(\varepsilon\), satisfies this target. A conditional computational obstruction alone does not prove the unconditional negative claim. Countably infinite or implicitly described references are outside this explicitly selected variant.

context_blocks.text: The source explicitly offers efficient evaluation from an explicit reference description as one meaning of a succinct functional. Binary rational inputs and polynomial bit complexity make that meaning a precise mathematical predicate. The broader closed-form and infinite-domain versions remain part of the source direction, and are not claimed equivalent to this variant.

Valiant and Valiant give reference-dependent bounds using the \(2/3\)-quasinorm of a vector after removal of its largest coordinate and a small-probability tail. Their theorem and following discussion explicitly permit constant-factor changes in the distance parameter as well as in the sample count. That is a different guarantee from a characterization at fixed \(\varepsilon\).

Canonne explains that the differing tail cutoffs can cause an arbitrarily large ratio between the resulting bounds, with harmonic probability profiles as an example. Section 2 discusses a second characterization using an interpolation functional, which has an analogous mismatch. Section 3 explains why bounds on the optimal separation radius up to constants do not automatically provide the requested fixed-distance sample characterization.

The source separately raises a proof-coverage issue for the earlier lower bound near point masses, and separates that repair as Open Question 3. It does not claim the lower-bound theorem false. Repairing that corner case alone would not close the characterization gap in Open Question 1. The present finite-domain definition also treats empty alternatives explicitly.
